questions.id: Increase difficulty by using a higher power for n.
questions.solution: The integral of x<sup>n</sup>e<sup>x</sup> is (x<sup>n+1</sup>e<sup>x</sup>)/(n+1)  + C. For n = 4, the solution is (x<sup>5</sup>e<sup>x</sup>)/5  + C.
questions.explanation: To integrate x<sup>4</sup>e<sup>x</sup>, use the power rule and multiply by the exponent plus one, then divide by the new exponent.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to add 1 to n when applying the power rule.

questions.id: Increase difficulty by using a negative exponent for n.
questions.solution: The integral of x<sup>n</sup>e<sup>x</sup> is (x<sup>n+1</sup>e<sup>x</sup>)/(n+1)  + C. For n = -2, the solution is (-x<sup>-3</sup>e<sup>x</sup>)/(-3)  + C.
questions.explanation: When integrating a negative exponent, remember to change the sign of the exponent before applying the power rule.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to change the sign of the exponent when it's negative.

questions.id: Increase difficulty by using a variable exponent for n.
questions.stem: Evaluate the integral ∫x<sup>a</sup>e<sup>x</sup>dx, where a is a constant
questions.solution: The integral of x<sup>n</sup>e<sup>x</sup> is (x<sup>n+1</sup>e<sup>x</sup>)/(n+1)  + C. For any constant a, the solution is (x<sup>a+1</sup>e<sup>x</sup>)/(a+1)  + C.
questions.explanation: The power rule applies regardless of whether n is a number or a variable.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to treat 'a' as if it were 1, forgetting that it's a constant.

questions.id: Increase difficulty by using integration by parts.
questions.solution: Use integration by parts: u = x<sup>2</sup>, dv = e<sup>x</sup>dx, du = 2xdx, v = e<sup>x</sup>. The integral becomes (x<sup>2</sup>e<sup>x</sup>) - ∫(2xe<sup>x</sup>)dx. Repeat integration by parts for the remaining integral: u = x, dv = e<sup>x</sup>dx, du = dx, v = e<sup>x</sup>. The final solution is e<sup>x</sup>(x<sup>2</sup> - x + 1)/3  + C.
questions.explanation: When the power of x is greater than 1, integration by parts may be required.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to perform a second round of integration by parts for the remaining integral.

questions.solution: Let u = 2x + 1, du = 2dx. The integral becomes (1/2)∫e<sup>u</sup>du = (1/2)e<sup>u</sup>/1 = (1/2)e<sup>2x+1</sup>  + C.
questions.explanation: Substitute the entire function inside the integral to simplify it before integrating.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to adjust the differential when making a substitution.

questions.id: Increase difficulty by using a trigonometric substitution.
questions.solution: Let x = sinθ, dx = cosθdθ. The integral becomes (cosθ)^2∫e<sup>cosθ</sup>cosθdθ. Use substitution: u = cosθ, du = -sinθdθ. The integral becomes -(1/3)e<sup>u</sup>(1  - u^2)^(3/2). Back-substitute to get the final solution: (1/6)e<sup>√(1-x^2)</sup>(1  - x<sup>2</sup>)^(3/2)  + C.
questions.explanation: When there's a square root involving 1  - x<sup>2</sup>, use a trigonometric substitution.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to change the limits of integration when using a trigonometric substitution.

questions.id: Increase difficulty by using partial fraction decomposition.
questions.solution: Decompose the fraction: x<sup>2</sup>/[(x+1)(x-2)] = A/(x+1) + B/(x-2). Solve for A and B, then integrate each term separately. The final solution is (1/3)e<sup>x</sup>(x  - 2) - (2/3)e<sup>x</sup>(x  + 1)  + C.
questions.explanation: When the denominator has multiple factors, use partial fraction decomposition before integrating.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget to multiply each term by e<sup>x</sup> after decomposing the fraction.
